old: Its ancient root once pointed to the very top of the head, not what's inside it.
In Dutch, the word for this organ is 'brein' — nearly a mirror of its English cousin.
West Frisian speakers call it 'brein,' a close echo of the English word it shares deep roots with.
clues: This organ of the body has been passed down in Germanic languages for over a thousand years without any documented shift in its meaning.
It fills your skull and handles thinking, memory and feeling, the physical organ rather than the abstract mind. An ancient Greek relative named the top of the head.
You rack it over a hard puzzle and call a clever friend this; Dutch and West Frisian speakers say brein.
